title: Textualism and enacted linguistic meaning
summary: Textualism gives controlling weight to the meaning of the enacted words in their relevant linguistic and legal context.
notes:
The approach protects the terms on which legislation actually secured enactment and resists substituting unenacted intentions or general policy aspirations. In Katzmann’s account, modern textualism uses context, established terms, ordinary usage, and conventions rather than treating dictionary definitions as invariably decisive. Criticism of legislative history also rests on bicameralism, presentment, and concerns about who speaks for the legislature.

Thomas’s Dolan and Small dissents illustrate disagreements over whether ordinary meaning already supplies a clear answer. Katzmann argues that excluding legislative history can discard useful evidence; textualists argue that using it can empower selective or unrepresentative statements. The existence of these disagreements does not mean every textualist always reaches one result, as Scalia’s vote in Dolan illustrates.
